summary: Defines an Anonymous mechanism for SASL, so services can offer anonymous login within that framework. It replaces the traditional practice of a plain-text password with the user name anonymous, which new IETF protocols do not permit. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A guest door where you can walk in without showing a name, replacing the old way of writing anonymous on a form.

questions: how does anonymous login work in sasl
what is the trace information in sasl anonymous
subtitle: A SASL login method that lets a client in without saying who it is, replacing the old 'anonymous' plain-text password trick.

tldr.problem: Services have long allowed anonymous access by having users log in with the name "anonymous" and an email address as the password. New IETF protocols do not permit plain-text login commands, so SASL needed its own way to do this.
tldr.mechanism: The ANONYMOUS mechanism is a single client message that may carry a short piece of trace information, either an email address or an opaque string of up to 255 characters, prepared with a "trace" stringprep profile.
tldr.outcome: It replaces RFC 2245, allows UTF-8 trace text instead of US-ASCII, and gives no security layer. The trace text is unauthenticated, so servers should keep anonymous access disabled by default and tightly restricted.

today: RFC 4505 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2006. It obsoletes RFC 2245, and the metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why SASL Needs an Anonymous Mechanism
sections.content:
On the Internet it is common to permit anonymous access to services. Traditionally this was done with a plain-text password mechanism: the user name was anonymous and the password was optional trace information such as an email address. Because plain-text login commands are not permitted in new IETF protocols, a new way to log in anonymously was needed inside the Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL) framework.

RFC 4505 defines a SASL mechanism named ANONYMOUS. Unlike most SASL mechanisms, which identify the user to the server, this one lets the user gain access without establishing or disclosing an identity. It does not provide a security layer.
sections.plainLanguage: Some places let anyone in as a guest. This document gives the guest door a proper, official shape so that newer systems can still offer it.

sections.title: The Single Client Message
sections.content:
The whole mechanism is one message from the client to the server. The message may carry trace information: a string of UTF-8 encoded Unicode characters prepared with the trace profile of stringprep. The trace information has no semantic value. It should be either an Internet email address or an opaque string that does not contain the @ character and that the system administrator of the client's domain can interpret.

The RFC gives a formal ABNF grammar: the message is an optional email address or token. A token is 1 to 255 characters, and since each UTF-8 character takes 1 to 4 octets, a token may be as long as 1020 octets.

A server that permits anonymous access announces support for ANONYMOUS and lets anyone log in with it, usually with restricted access. For privacy, an email address or other identifying information should only be used with the user's permission.
sections.plainLanguage: The guest just hands over one small note, which can be empty. The note is only a hint for the staff, and the guest should only put their real email on it if they want to.

sections.title: The "trace" Stringprep Profile
sections.content:
To say exactly which characters may appear in the trace text, the RFC defines a stringprep profile called trace. Its character repertoire is Unicode 3.2. No mapping and no Unicode normalization are required, and unassigned code points are not prohibited.

The profile prohibits characters from these stringprep tables: C.2.1 and C.2.2 (control characters), C.3 (private use), C.4 (non-character code points), C.5 (surrogate codes), C.6 (inappropriate for plain text), C.8 (change display properties are deprecated) and C.9 (tagging characters). No other characters are prohibited. The profile also requires bidirectional character checking as described in Section 6 of stringprep.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a list of letters and symbols that are not allowed on the note, such as invisible control characters, so that every system reads the note the same way.

sections.title: An IMAP Login Example
sections.content:
The RFC shows an anonymous login between an IMAP client and server. The server lists AUTH=ANONYMOUS among its capabilities, the client sends AUTHENTICATE ANONYMOUS, the server answers with an empty + continuation, and the client sends its trace information, here the string sirhc, base64 encoded as c2lyaGM=. The server then replies that trace information has been logged.

The base64 encoding and the + prefix belong to the IMAP profile of SASL, not to SASL itself. Protocols that allow an initial client response can skip the extra round trip.
sections.plainLanguage: The guest tells the doorman they want to come in as a guest, the doorman says go ahead, the guest hands over a note, and the doorman writes it in the logbook.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Since the mechanism grants access to anyone, it should be disabled by default so the administrator makes an explicit decision to enable it. Several risks follow:

  • If anonymous users can write, someone can fill all available space. Disabling anonymous write access prevents this.
  • If anonymous users can both read and write the same area, the server becomes an anonymous communication channel. Servers that accept anonymous submissions should use the common "drop box" model, which forbids anonymous read access to the submission area.
  • Expensive operations, such as an IMAP SEARCH BODY, can enable denial of service, so servers are encouraged to lower the priority of anonymous users or limit their resources. Limiting the number of anonymous users can itself enable denial of service and should be used with caution.

The trace information is not authenticated, so it can be falsified, and investigators of abuse need to remember that. Clients should not send the user's email address without explicit permission and should offer the option of sending no trace information, which exposes only the source IP address and time. Anonymous connections are also open to man-in-the-middle attacks, so clients and servers are encouraged to support external data security services.

The RFC adds that protocols which do not require an explicit anonymous login are more susceptible to break-ins, and that protocols offering restricted data access should not allow anonymous data access without an explicit login step.
sections.plainLanguage: If anyone can walk in, you must decide to open that door on purpose, keep guests away from the valuables, and remember that a name on a guest's note may be made up.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The IANA entry for the ANONYMOUS SASL mechanism was updated so that it points to this document as its technical specification, with intended usage COMMON. The RFC also registers the new stringprep profile trace, first defined here.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of SASL mechanisms was updated to point at this document, and the new note-writing rules were added to the list of stringprep profiles.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 2245
sections.content: RFC 2245 allowed an optional human-readable trace string but restricted it to US-ASCII. Because the Internet is international, RFC 4505 uses UTF-8 encoded Unicode and defines the trace stringprep profile to say precisely which characters are allowed. The string is still limited to 255 characters, but each character may now be 1 to 4 octets long. A number of editorial changes were also made.
sections.plainLanguage: The old version only allowed plain English letters on the note. The new one allows writing in many languages, with clear rules about which symbols are fine.
